profile.summary: This is the retrieval evaluation reported in the MSAlign paper, not a separate suite. Given a tandem mass spectrum and a candidate set of 256 molecules pulled from PubChem by mass, a method must rank the true structure first; recall at 1, 5 and 20 is reported. The current version of the paper scores Spectraverse and MassSpecGym under two splits, a chemical-formula split the authors recommend and MassSpecGym's harder MCES split, and reports methods that need the target formula separately from those that do not. It is for developers of spectrum-to-structure methods who need results that are comparable across models and splits.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is molecule retrieval from a tandem mass spectrum: the method scores each molecule in a candidate set against the spectrum, and is judged on whether the true structure appears at the top of the ranking. The paper frames this as the tractable version of metabolite identification, and treats the choice of data split as part of what is being measured, because splits trade leakage against distribution shift. A second contribution is therefore a measure of how far a split moves the test distribution from the training distribution.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The current version uses two open benchmarks: MassSpecGym, 231,104 curated and standardised spectrum and molecule pairs, and Spectraverse, 488,797 pairs with broader coverage of adducts and ionisation modes, more than half of its spectra from adducts other than [M+H]+. The paper warns that pair counts overstate chemical diversity because the same molecule recurs under different ionisation conditions, and gives unique molecule counts in an appendix table. The first version of the paper also used NPLIB1, the smallest benchmark at 10,633 spectrum and molecule pairs. Candidate sets follow MassSpecGym's standardised protocol: molecules are drawn from PubChem's 118M compounds whose mass matches the target within 10 ppm, prioritising databases of decreasing metabolite relevance, and the pool is cut to 256 candidates per spectrum, which the paper says are typically structurally close to the target.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Recall at 1, 5 and 20 over the 256-candidate pool is the reported metric, higher is better. Methods that assume the target's molecular formula is known are reported in a separate block, because in practice the formula has to be estimated; MSAlign is also run in that setting by filtering candidates to those matching the ground-truth formula, which cuts the pool to about 100. The main split is by chemical formula, so that train, validation and test molecules have distinct formulas, with results averaged over three random seeds of the splitting algorithm; MassSpecGym's official MCES split is reported as well, averaged over its two variants obtained by swapping validation and test, because generating new MCES splits is expensive and the validation set is used for calibration and checkpoint selection. The repository states the ranking rules: candidate 0 is the target, padded candidates score minus infinity, a negative tied with the target ranks ahead of it, fusion weights are calibrated on validation data and metrics come from test data, and results across splits are macro-averaged.

sections.title: The split-shift measure
sections.body: Rather than argue about splits, the paper measures them. Each spectrum and molecule pair is encoded as the concatenation of an L2-normalised spectrum embedding and an L2-normalised molecule embedding, and the sliced Wasserstein distance between the training and test distributions is computed with the POT library using 100 random projections, then divided by the value from a random split so that a random split scores 1. On MassSpecGym the MCES and Murcko splits induce the largest shift and the formula and 2D InChIKey splits sit in between; the authors recommend the formula split because it is strictly more challenging than InChIKey, two molecules with the same InChIKey necessarily having the same formula, and still reflects deployment. The repository exposes this as its own command.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository reproduces both the MSAlign models and the baselines. Datasets are downloaded and prepared per split and seed, or the prepared archives are downloaded from Zenodo with a checksum check. The four frozen input representations (DreaMS spectra, MolDeBERTa molecules, Morgan fingerprints, with spectrum bins computed on demand) are precomputed on a GPU, MolDeBERTa being a gated Hugging Face model that needs its terms accepted and a token set. One command then trains a model on one split, another evaluates the selected checkpoint once on the test candidates, and a third calibrates and evaluates the score fusion. A separate playground environment scores a spectrum against candidate SMILES from a pretrained checkpoint without any training data.

The main split is by chemical formula, so train, validation and test molecules have distinct formulas, averaged over three random seeds of the splitting algorithm; the repository prepares five seeds, formula_seed0 to formula_seed4. facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split itself, and it is measured rather than asserted. Molecules in train, validation and test have distinct chemical formulas in the main setting, which the paper argues is strictly stronger than an InChIKey split, and the induced distribution shift is quantified by the normalised sliced Wasserstein distance. The paper's point is that stricter splits such as MCES prevent leakage at the cost of a large shift, with MCES test sets forming a distinct cluster away from the training data.

run_guide.summary: Prepare one dataset and split, precompute the frozen representations, train the model on that split, and evaluate the selected checkpoint once on the test candidates.
prerequisites: Python 3.11 and uv, and a CUDA GPU; the graph baselines need a DGL wheel built for Linux, Python 3.11 and CUDA 12.1.
Access to the gated MolDeBERTa model on Hugging Face, with its terms accepted and HF_TOKEN set.
Multiple CPU cores for building the candidate sets, or the prepared archives from Zenodo instead.
The repository code is MIT; the prepared data on Zenodo are CC BY 4.0, and the external datasets and pretrained models keep their own licences.

notes: This record is one paper's evaluation. The version matters: version 1 (2026-05-19) reports four arms, NPLIB1, Spectraverse, MassSpecGym formula split and MassSpecGym MCES split, with baselines including FFN and SAIL; version 3 (2026-11-02) drops NPLIB1, reports three arms and a different baseline set, and renames the fused model. The record's protocol list includes NPLIB1 arms and entries labelled MSAlign v2; no saved file here uses the label v2, so those are left unmatched. Sizes are whole-dataset pair counts as the paper prints them, not test-set sizes, which the paper does not give in the text read; the candidate pool is 256 per spectrum, or about 100 for the formula-filtered variant. The store's existing source is the unversioned arXiv PDF address, which now serves version 3. Figures cannot be compared across different candidate sets, as the paper states for NPLIB1.
